children.label: The Age of Social Change
French Revolution Impact
Ideas of freedom and equality
Possibility of societal change
Influence in Europe and Asia (e.g., Raja Rammohan Roy)
Societal Divisions in Europe
Industrial Society & Social Change
New cities, industrialised regions, railways, Industrial Revolution
Impact of Industrialisation
Liberals & Radicals' Role
Searched for solutions
Often property owners/employers
Believed in individual effort, labour, enterprise
Rallied working class for change
Revolutionaries (Nationalists, Liberals, Radicals)
Wanted to end 1815 European governments
Overthrow monarchs (France, Italy, Germany, Russia)
Create 'nations' with equal rights (e.g., Giuseppe Mazzini)
The Coming of Socialism to Europe
Far-reaching vision of societal structure
Socialist Principles
Against private property (root of social ills)
Collective control of property for social interests
Campaign for change
Visions of the Future
Cooperative Idea
Robert Owen (New Harmony, USA)
Louis Blanc (Government encouragement of cooperatives)
Marxist Socialism/Communism
Karl Marx & Friedrich Engels (Communist Manifesto)
Industrial society is capitalist
Capitalists profit from workers
Workers must overthrow capitalism and private property
Radically socialist society (socially controlled property)
Communist society (natural society of future)
Support for Socialism
Spread throughout Europe by 1870s
Formation of Second International (1889)
Worker associations (England, Germany) for rights
Social Democratic Party (Germany) winning seats
Labour Party (Britain, 1905), Socialist Party (France, 1905)
No socialist government in Europe until 1914
Paris Commune of 1871 (workers' red flag, 'Marseillaise')
The Russian Revolution
Socialists took over government in October Revolution 1917
Fall of monarchy in February 1917
Russian Empire in 1914
Ruled by Tsar Nicholas II
Vast territory (Finland, Latvia, Poland, Central Asia, etc.)
Majority Russian Orthodox, also Catholics, Protestants, Muslims, Buddhists
Economy and Society (Pre-1917)
Majority agriculturists (85%)
Russia as major grain exporter
Industry
Found in pockets (St Petersburg, Moscow)
Craftsmen and large factories
Growth in 1890s (railways, foreign investment)
Most industry private property
Workers' Conditions
Long hours, poor wages (craftsmen 15h, factories 10-12h)
Accommodation in rooms/dormitories
Divided social group (village links vs. permanent city dwellers)
Divided by skill (metalworkers 'aristocrats')
Women 31% of factory labour, paid less
Associations for aid, but few
Strikes frequent (textile 1896-97, metal 1902)
Peasant Conditions
Cultivated most land, but nobility/crown/church owned large properties
Divided, deeply religious
No respect for nobility (unlike France)
Wanted noble land, refused rent, murdered landlords
Unique land pooling custom (mir/commune)
Socialism in Russia (Pre-1914)
All political parties illegal
Russian Social Democratic Workers Party (1898)
Founded by George Plekhanov (Marxist ideas)
Operated illegally, newspaper, mobilised workers, organised strikes
Socialist Revolutionary Party (1900)
Believed peasants (land division custom) were natural socialists
Struggled for peasant rights, demanded noble land transfer
Disagreements on Peasants (Lenin)
Peasants not united (poor, rich, labourers, capitalists)
Could not all be part of socialist movement
Party Organisation Strategy
Bolsheviks (Lenin): Disciplined, controlled membership in repressive society
Mensheviks (Alexander Kerensky/Martov, Plekhanov, Trotsky): Open to all
1905 Revolution (Turbulent Time)
Causes
Poor conditions for workers (1904: prices rose, wages declined 20%)
Dismissal of 4 Assembly of Russian Workers members at Putilov Iron Works
Russo-Japanese War defeat (1904) - fatal blow to prestige, anti-Tsar feelings
Events
Strikes by 110,000+ workers in St Petersburg (8-hour day, higher wages, better conditions)
Bloody Sunday (Jan 9, 1905): Peaceful workers led by Father Gapon fired upon near Winter Palace (1000+ killed, 300 wounded)
Strikes, university closures, civil liberties demands
Union of Unions (lawyers, doctors, engineers) demanded constituent assembly
Outcomes
Tsar allowed elected consultative Parliament (Duma)
Brief existence of trade unions/factory committees (later illegal)
Tsar dismissed first two Dumas, packed third with conservatives
Birth of Soviets (council of workers' representatives) - instruments of political power
First World War & Russian Empire (1914-1917)
Central powers (Germany, Austria, Turkey) vs. Allied powers (France, Britain, Russia)
Impact on Russia
Initially popular, but Tsar refused Duma consultation
Tsarina's German origins & poor advisors (Rasputin) made autocracy unpopular
Eastern front different (mobile battles, large casualties)
Armies lost badly (7 million casualties by 1917)
Retreating army destroyed crops/buildings (3 million refugees)
Discredited government and Tsar, soldiers unwilling to fight
Severe impact on industry (few, cut off by Baltic Sea, equipment disintegrated)
Railway lines broke down (1916), labour shortages, workshops shut
Grain to army, bread/flour scarce in cities, bread riots (winter 1916)
February Revolution in Petrograd (1917)
Grim conditions in capital (Petrograd) - food shortages
Winter of 1917: very cold, frost, heavy snow
Parliamentarians opposed Tsar's desire to dissolve Duma
Key Events
Feb 22 (Mar 7): Lockout at factory on right bank
Feb 23 (Mar 8): 50 factories strike in sympathy (International Women's Day)
Demonstrators to Nevskii Prospekt, government curfew
Feb 25 (Mar 10): Government suspended Duma, politicians spoke out
Feb 27 (Mar 12): Police Headquarters ransacked, slogans for bread, wages, hours, democracy
Cavalry refused to fire, regiments mutinied, joined striking workers
Soldiers and workers formed Petrograd Soviet in Duma building
Mar 1 (Mar 14): Delegation to Tsar, military advised abdication
Mar 2 (Mar 15): Tsar Nicholas II abdicated, end of Romanov dynasty
Immediate Aftermath
Provisional Government formed (Soviet and Duma leaders)
Russia's future by constituent assembly (universal adult suffrage)
Dual Power system (Provisional Government + Petrograd Soviet)
After February (April 1917 - October 1917)
Provisional Government: Army officials, landowners, industrialists influential
Restrictions on public meetings/associations removed
Soviets set up everywhere
Lenin's Return & April Theses
Returned from exile in April 1917
Time for Soviets to take power
Demands: War close, land to peasants, banks nationalised
Bolshevik Party rename to Communist Party
Spreading Workers' Movement
Factory committees questioned industrialist control
Trade unions grew, soldiers' committees formed
All Russian Congress of Soviets (June)
Provisional Government Response
Power reduced, Bolshevik influence grew
Resisted workers' control, arrested leaders
Repressed pro-Bolshevik demonstrations (July 1917)
Bolshevik leaders went into hiding
Peasants seized land (July-September 1917) encouraged by Socialist Revolutionaries
October Revolution (Bolshevik Revolution) 1917
Conflict between Provisional Government & Bolsheviks grew
Lenin feared dictatorship, discussed uprising
Key Events
Oct 16: Lenin persuaded Petrograd Soviet/Bolshevik Party to seize power
Military Revolutionary Committee (Leon Trotskii) appointed to organise
Oct 24: Uprising began
PM Kerenskii left city to summon troops
Pro-government troops seized Bolshevik newspaper buildings, guarded Winter Palace
MRC ordered supporters to seize government offices, arrest ministers
Ship Aurora shelled Winter Palace
City under committee control, ministers surrendered
All-Russian Congress of Soviets approved Bolshevik action
Heavy fighting in other cities (especially Moscow), Bolsheviks controlled Moscow-Petrograd by December
What Changed After October?
Bolsheviks opposed private property
Nationalisation of industry and banks (Nov 1917)
Land declared social property, peasants seized noble land
Partition of large houses in cities
Banned old aristocracy titles, new uniforms (budeonovka)
Bolshevik Party renamed Russian Communist Party (Bolshevik)
Failed to gain majority in Constituent Assembly elections (Nov 1917)
Lenin dismissed Assembly (Jan 1918) - All Russian Congress of Soviets seen as more democratic
Peace with Germany at Brest Litovsk (March 1918)
Russia became one-party state (Bolsheviks only party in elections)
Trade unions under party control
Secret police (Cheka, OGPU, NKVD) punished critics
Experiments in arts/architecture, but censorship disillusioned many
Civil War (1918-1920)
Land redistribution led to army breakup (peasants deserted for land)
Non-Bolshevik socialists, liberals, pro-Tsarists ('greens' & 'whites') condemned uprising
Leaders moved to south Russia, organised troops against Bolsheviks ('reds')
Backed by France, America, Britain, Japan (worried about socialism)
Looting, banditry, famine became common
'Whites' took harsh steps with peasants, lost popular support
By Jan 1920, Bolsheviks controlled most of former Russian empire
Cooperation with non-Russian nationalities and Muslim jadidists
Creation of Soviet Union (USSR) in Dec 1922
Political autonomy for non-Russian nationalities, but unpopular policies (e.g., discouragement of nomadism)
Making a Socialist Society
Industries and banks nationalised during Civil War
Peasants cultivated socialised land
Bolsheviks used confiscated land for collective work demonstration
Centralised Planning (Five-Year Plans)
Officials assessed economy, set 5-year targets
Government fixed prices to promote industrial growth (1927-32, 1933-38)
Economic growth: oil, coal, steel production increased 100% (1929-33)
New factory cities (e.g., Magnitogorsk)
Poor working conditions (550 stoppages in Magnitogorsk first year)
Extended schooling, university access for workers/peasants
Creches in factories for women workers' children
Cheap public healthcare, model living quarters (uneven due to limited resources)
Stalinism and Collectivisation
Lenin died Jan 1924, Joseph Stalin took power
1927-28: Acute grain shortages in towns
Government fixed grain prices, peasants refused to sell
Stalin's belief: Rich peasants (kulaks) holding stocks for higher prices
1928: Party members enforced grain collections, raided kulaks
Decision to collectivise farms due to small holdings, inability to modernise
Eliminate kulaks, take land, establish state-controlled large farms
Collectivisation Programme (from 1929)
Peasants forced to cultivate in collective farms (kolkhoz)
Land/implements transferred to collective ownership, profits shared
Enraged peasants resisted, destroyed livestock (cattle fell 1/3, 1929-31)
Resisters severely punished (deported, exiled)
Allowed some independent cultivation but treated unsympathetically
Did not increase production immediately
Bad harvests (1930-33) led to devastating famine (over 4 million died)
Party critics (industrial production, collectivisation) charged with conspiracy
By 1939: 2 million in prisons/labour camps, false confessions under torture, executions of talented professionals
Great Purge: Millions arrested/murdered, villages burnt, villagers killed/evicted
Global Influence of Russian Revolution and USSR
Promotion of Socialism and Communism worldwide
Formation of Communist parties in most countries (e.g., Great Britain, India)
Communist governments established (Poland, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, China)
Bolsheviks encouraged colonial peoples
Comintern (international union of pro-Bolshevik socialist parties) 1919
Communist University of Workers of the East (USSR)
Redefinition of Democracy: Political democracy meaningless without social/economic equality
Rights of Workers: United workers globally, enhanced prestige
Rise of Nationalism: Weakened imperialism, inspired Asian/African peoples
Encouraged struggle between Capitalists and Workers
Division of World and Cold War: Two blocs (socialist vs. capitalist)
Criticisms & Realities
Existing socialist parties didn't wholly approve Bolshevik methods
By 1950s, USSR government style not aligned with revolutionary ideals
Developed into great power, industry/agriculture grew, poor fed
Denied essential freedoms, used repressive policies
International reputation declined by late 20th century
Socialist ideals still respected, rethought in different ways
